title: Evals ops workbook: dataset loaders, scoring snippets, and CI recipes
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a practical ops-focused workbook for onboarding new models into the eval harness. It captures implementation patterns we've iterated on for loaders, small reusable scoring snippets, and the CI wiring we use to make regression checks automatic.

Why this doc exists (notes to self):
- People keep re-implementing slightly different dataset loaders and scorer wrappers — causes flaky CI and inconsistent metrics.
- Goal: provide a minimal, copy-pasteable set of patterns that work for our typical onboarding flows (generation, classification, reranking, embeddings).
- Keep it lightweight: recipes prefer simple python files + pytest over heavy frameworks.

Repo layout (convention used by eval-harness repo):
- evals/                  # top-level harness code
- evals/loaders/          # dataset loader modules (one per dataset type)
- evals/scorers/          # scoring functions + small wrappers
- evals/tests/            # unit+integration tests for datasets and metrics
- evals/ci/               # CI helper scripts (sanity checks, example runs)
- ci/                     # GitHub Actions workflows (calls evals/ci)

Key loader patterns (copyable):
1) Simple JSONL QA loader (single-turn generation):
- Expectation: line-delimited JSON where each item has {"id", "input", "target"}.
- Minimal loader: iterates lines, yields dict with fields 'example_id', 'prompt', 'references'.
- Example snippet: 
  def load_jsonl_qagen(path):
      with open(path, 'r') as f:
          for i, line in enumerate(f):
              j = json.loads(line)
              yield {
                  'example_id': j.get('id', f'line-{i}'),
                  'prompt': j['input'],
                  'references': [j['target']]
              }
- Tests: small fixtures with 3 examples; assert loader yields correct keys and fallback id behavior.

2) Multi-shot chat-style loader (alternating roles):
- Handle arrays of messages, convert to single string prompt using our canonical joiner ("\n---\n").
- Preserve role labels when evaluator needs them.

3) Reranking / IR-format loader:
- Input contains a 'query' and a list of candidate passages. We flatten into per-candidate examples with a relevance label.
- For efficiency in scoring, include a group_id field so reranker metrics can compute groupwise MRR/NDCG.

4) Embeddings-based eval loader:
- Load pairs/triplets for cosine-sim tasks. Store precomputed reference embeddings path in metadata (s3://redwood-evals/... ) so CI doesn't need to re-embed heavy corpora.

Scorer recipes (minimal, deterministic where possible):
A) Exact match (generation tasks):
- Normalization: unicode normalize, lower, strip, collapse whitespace, optionally remove punctuation.
- Score: 1 if any normalized reference == normalized prediction else 0.
- Use-case: closed-ended dataset onboarding (F1 not needed).

B) Token F1 (QA extractive):
- Tokenize on whitespace + simple punctuation split. Compute precision/recall/F1 per example.
- Edge case: when both empty => score 1.

C) Embedding similarity (semantic retrieval):
- If references are long passages, compute cosine similarity between predicted embedding and reference embedding set. Max similarity becomes example score.
- Use precomputed embeddings where possible in CI to keep latency low.

D) Classification accuracy + per-class confusion logging:
- Return scalar accuracy and small failure sample list (max 10 per class) saved as JSON artifact for human review.

E) Reranking metrics (MRR / NDCG):
- Group by query_id, compute ranks, handle tie-breaking deterministically by candidate id.

Metric wrapper conventions:
- All scorers should implement a stable function signature: score_example(example, prediction) -> {"score": float, "details": str}  (we store details as short strings).
- Top-level aggregator takes list of example-level scores and returns a dict of aggregate metrics plus a small failures.json file path.

Regression reports and artifact conventions:
- Every eval run (CI or nightly) should emit a JSON report with:
  - run_id, model_version, commit_sha, dataset, num_examples, metrics (flat map), failures_path, runtime_seconds, host_tag
- Failures artifact: NDJSON lines with example_id, prompt snippet, prediction snippet, score, reference_snippet. Keep snippets <= 400 chars.
- Store artifacts under s3://redwood-evals/runs/{run_id}/ report.json + failures.ndjson + raw-predictions.jsonl

CI wiring (Github Actions + pytest recipes):
1) Unit tests (fast, run on PRs):
- tests/loaders/* : small fixtures for each loader (10–50 examples), sanity checks on keys/ids.
- tests/scorers/* : deterministic inputs -> known outputs.
- Run: pytest -q tests/unit (should be <30s).

2) Lightweight integration smoke (run on merges to main or daily):
- evals/ci/smoke_run.py runs a 50-example eval with a canned lightweight model stub (we have a model-mock package that returns deterministic outputs).
- This validates end-to-end wiring (loader -> evaluation -> report).
- Smoke run outputs to a temp S3 path and publishes a brief comment to the PR via a GH action step if it fails thresholds.

3) Full regression job (scheduled/nightly for master):
- Runs 500–2000 examples depending on dataset. Compares metrics against baseline stored in s3://redwood-evals/benchmarks/{dataset}/baseline.json.
- If any metric regresses beyond allowed delta, fail the job and open JIRA-MLEVAL-REGRESSION auto-ticket with run artifacts attached.

Threshold gating examples:
- For generation: allow -0.02 absolute decrease in exact-match, -0.05 in F1.
- For embeddings retrieval: allow -0.015 in mean cosine.
- Thresholds configurable by dataset in a small dataset-metadata.yaml kept alongside the dataset.

Practical tips for local dev:
- Use --local-cache to point to a small precomputed embeddings file to avoid re-embedding.
- Use model-mock to simulate latency and deterministic outputs: pip install git+https://github.com/redwood-inference/model-mock.git
- Example local run: python -m evals.ci.run_single --dataset tests/fixtures/qagen-small.jsonl --scorer exact_match --model model_mock:deterministic --out runs/local-debug.json

Performance considerations:
- Keep loaders memory-light: stream JSONL instead of loading full file.
- Scorers that need tokenization should reuse a shared tokenizer instance (module-level) to avoid repeated init cost in CI.
- For large datasets in nightly runs, use chunked evaluation and incremental upload of artifacts to S3 to avoid ephemeral disk pressure.

Common pitfalls we keep seeing:
- Different normalization rules between scorer and reference generation -> false regressions. Fix: single util normalize_text used everywhere.
- Test fixtures too small — flakiness appears only at scale. Solution: include one medium-sized fixture (200–500 examples) in evals/tests/large_fixtures/ but mark it to only run in nightly.
- Relying on live hosted models in PR CI — leads to rate limit blowups. Use model-mock in PRs.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we adopt a standard tokenization library (sacremoses / tiktoken) across all scorers? Pros: consistency, cons: dependency/CI install time.
- Add a small binary that validates dataset schemas via jsonschema and expose as pre-commit hook. (JIRA-MLEVAL-99)
- Create a tiny JS-based scorer for quick in-browser inspection of failures for product review.

Example quick checklist for a model onboarding PR:
- [ ] Add dataset loader into evals/loaders/ with unit test in tests/loaders/
- [ ] Add scorer (if nontrivial) with tests in tests/scorers/
- [ ] Add dataset-metadata.yaml entry (baseline path, gating thresholds)
- [ ] Add CI smoke recipe entry in evals/ci/smoke_registry.py
- [ ] Run local smoke (see local dev example) and attach runs/local-debug.json to PR

Appendix: Useful snippets and references:
- loader unit test pattern: assert list(loader(path))[0].keys() == {'example_id','prompt','references'}
- scorer test: assert scorer.score_example(fixture_example, fixture_prediction)["score"] == 1.0
- GH Actions: use reuseable workflow .github/workflows/eval-smoke.yml with inputs dataset-path, model-ref, out-s3-path.

Contact / ownership:
- Claire Zhang (owner) — eng-applied-ml
- Collab: Miguel Santos (scorers), Asha Patel (ci/infra)

Last notes: treat this doc as a living workbook. When you copy a pattern into a PR, try to keep code intentionally small and link back to this file so future contributors find canonical examples.
